title: Human-in-the-Loop Systems for Adaptive Learning Using Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how generative AI can be made more adaptive and educationally useful by moving beyond one-shot chatbot responses. The authors argue that most educational LLM systems are static and do not allow students to actively shape the system’s behavior. To address this, they propose a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) adaptive learning framework in which students critique AI-generated responses using structured feedback tags, with the goal of improving personalization, engagement, and learning support in STEM contexts.

The intervention is a modular web-based tutoring system that runs four parallel pipelines for comparison: Personalized + Feedback, Personalized, RAG, and a plain LLM baseline. Students first complete an onboarding questionnaire about experience, learning style, design challenges, and goals. During interaction, they can rate responses using five feedback tags ranging from “Excellent” to “Terrible.” These signals are incorporated into prompt engineering and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline that retrieves textbook passages and adjusts later responses. The system was implemented for Object-Oriented Design tutoring, with about 200 conversational turns across eight sessions.

The population studied was STEM students in a university context, specifically in Object-Oriented Design, and the institutional affiliation suggests the study was conducted at North Carolina State University in the United States. The paper does not report random assignment or a formal experimental participant design; instead, it compares outputs generated by multiple system pipelines on the same conversational turns and evaluates them using a GPT-based scorer on correctness, clarity, readability, and adaptability.

The main conclusions are that static personalization based on onboarding metadata produced the strongest adaptability scores, while retrieval grounding produced the highest factual correctness and substantially outperformed the plain LLM baseline on accuracy. Live feedback tagging showed only modest benefits, largely because students used feedback infrequently and the tag scheme was coarse and applied only at the end of turns. The authors conclude that combining stable user profiling with retrieval is promising for adaptive learning, but that richer and more immediate feedback mechanisms are needed for stronger student-in-the-loop personalization.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A human-in-the-loop generative AI tutoring framework that combines onboarding-based personalization, student feedback tags, and retrieval-augmented generation to adapt instructional responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a modular web-based tutoring system for Object-Oriented Design/STEM learning, comparing four pipelines: Personalized+Feedback, Personalized, RAG, and a plain LLM baseline across approximately 200 conversational turns in eight sessions.

findings.finding_summary: Across approximately 200 conversational turns over eight sessions, GPT-based evaluation showed that the Personalized pipeline achieved the highest Adaptability score (5.43/10), followed by Personalized + Feedback (4.55), RAG (4.12), and LLM (2.78). This indicates personalization improved alignment to learner needs, but adding sparse end-of-turn feedback tags did not outperform static onboarding metadata.
findings.measure: GPT-based Adaptability ratings (1-10) of pipeline responses

findings.finding_summary: The retrieval-grounded and personalized variants outperformed the plain LLM baseline on correctness in Object-Oriented Design tutoring. Mean Correctness scores were 9.81 for Personalized, 9.70 for RAG, 8.65 for Personalized + Feedback, and 7.89 for LLM on a 1-10 GPT-based rubric.
findings.measure: GPT-based Correctness ratings (1-10) of tutoring responses

findings.finding_summary: All four pipelines produced similarly strong clarity and readability scores, suggesting prompt design rather than adaptation mechanism drove these qualities. Mean Clarity ranged from 8.03 to 8.95 and Readability ranged from 7.83 to 8.88 across the four conditions.
findings.measure: GPT-based Clarity and Readability ratings (1-10) of pipeline responses

findings.finding_summary: Student engagement with the live feedback mechanism was limited: only 19 feedback tags were recorded across all turns, with counts of Excellent=3, Very Helpful=5, Average=6, Poor=3, and Terrible=2. The paper concludes that sparse usage and coarse end-of-turn tags likely limited real-time improvement from the Human-in-the-Loop feedback design.
findings.measure: Turn-level usage of live feedback tags

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparison of system variants, but it appears to be a preliminary study with approximately 200 turns across eight sessions, no randomized controlled design, and outcomes scored by a GPT-based evaluator rather than validated human or external assessments.
impact_tier_rationale: Results suggest promising but unclear impact: personalized and RAG variants scored higher than the plain LLM baseline on system-rated correctness and adaptability, but no standardized learning effect sizes, confidence intervals, or direct student achievement gains were reported.
